15.0.s.en: 1. Taking pride in the merciful God

15.0.0.en: 1 But You, our God, are gracious and true, longsuffering, and in mercy ordering all things. 2 For if we sin, we are Yours, knowing Your power; but we will not sin, knowing that we are counted Yours. 3 For to know You is perfect righteousness, and to know Your power is the root of immortality.

15.0.1.en: But You, our God, are good and true, longsuffering, and ordering all things in mercy. [1]

15.0.2.en: In the midst of his speaking of the idol worship which shattered man's thought with folly, and his life with abominations and lying with violence and cruelty, Solomon looked to God to see a joyful, shining picture. So he speaks of Him as “our God,” as though the pagans possess idols as their property, but they cannot possess or own them, for they are lifeless. But God is our God who possesses us as a people for Himself, takes pride in us, and we take pride in Him.

15.0.3.en: We saw that with corruption pagan worship was marked by violence and fierceness until it reached the offering of human sacrifices, but our God is good, true in His promises, longsuffering, the Upholder of all, ordering all things for our benefit and our eternal edification.

15.0.4.en: The author presents his discussion of the punishment of the wicked in the form of a prayer addressed to God (Wis 15:2-3), who is merciful and mighty, in contrast to the idols which are utterly unable to act.

15.0.5.en: David the prophet had already sung, saying: “For You, Lord, are good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon You... But You, O Lord, are a God full of compassion, and gracious, longsuffering, and plenteous in mercy and truth” (Ps 86:5, 15).

15.1.0.en: And even if we sin we are Yours, knowing Your power; but we will not choose to sin, knowing that we are counted as Yours. [2]

15.1.1.en: The author confesses that Israel sinned by turning aside to idol worship, but since he realizes that he is the people of God he finds the door of repentance open before him to enjoy God's mercies, believing in God's power to save even from idol worship. The secret of his falling into idol worship is two things:

15.1.2.en: First: his ignorance that he is God's own.

15.1.3.en: Second: his not realizing that God is perfect righteousness and the Almighty and the root of immortality.

15.1.4.en: In other words, what preserves us from sin, and what drives us to repentance when we have sinned, is our realization of our position in relation to God, that we are His own, beloved by Him and cared for by Him. The second matter is the truth of God's person, that He is our Father who does not withhold from us but gives Himself to us, and He is the supreme righteousness, the Almighty and the Giver of immortality. So while we constantly feel our weakness, our position gives us cleaving to Him and belonging to Him, and our knowledge of His truth gives us boldness to ask as befits His possibilities, to become an icon of Him, bearing His righteousness and trusting in His power and hoping for eternity.

15.1.5.en: * It was necessary that they should come up by means of the water in order to become alive, for they cannot enter the Kingdom of God unless they put off the state of death that they had before... For before a man bears the name “Son of God” he is dead, but when he receives the seal he casts off the state of death and enjoys life. The seal then is the water, into which they go down dead and come up alive.

15.1.6.en: Father Hermas * Truly we go down into the water full of sins and defilement, and come up bearing fruit in our hearts, bearing in our spirits the fear (of God) and hope in Jesus.

15.2.0.en: St. Barnabas For to know who You are is perfect righteousness, and to know Your power is the root of immortality. [3]

15.2.1.en: St. John the Beloved explains to us this phrase together with the preceding one, saying: “Behold, what manner of love the Father has bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God... Whosoever abides in Him sins not: whosoever sins has not seen Him, neither known Him... Whosoever is born of God does not commit sin; for His seed remains in him: and he cannot sin, because he is born of God. In this the children of God are manifest, and the children of the devil: whosoever does not righteousness is not of God” (1 Jn 3:1, 6, 9-10).

15.2.2.en: * We must hasten to know what way leads to the forgiveness of sins and the hope of the inheritance of the good things promised, for there is no other way but this: that you come to know this Christ, and be washed in the fountain (Baptism) of which Isaiah spoke for the forgiveness of sins (Isa 4:4), and so we begin to live in holiness.

15.2.3.en: Justin the Martyr * Since you were baptized into Christ, and have put on Christ, you have become subject to the Son of God... By this you become partakers of Christ.

15.3.s.en: 2. Idolatry, the fruit of corruption and folly

15.3.0.en: 4 For neither did the mischievous invention of men's art deceive us, nor the painter's fruitless labor, a form stained with divers colors; 5 the sight whereof entices fools to lust, so that they desire the form of a dead image that has no breath. 6 Both they that make them, and they that desire them, and they that worship them, are lovers of evil things, and are worthy to have such things to trust upon.

15.3.1.en: For neither did what the wicked art of men invented lead us astray, nor the barren labors of painters, images smeared with discordant colors. [4]

15.3.2.en: In his book Contra Gentes (Against the Pagans) St. Athanasius the Apostolic says that evil had no existence; it is made by the evil will of man. God did not create evil, but man's withdrawal from God, who is wholly good, drove him to evil. This evil is the origin of idol worship, which had no existence, but came as a natural result of the evil brought into being by the evil will.

15.3.3.en: But the children of God, whose thoughts are lifted up to the heavens, however far the creativity of artists reaches, their hearts cannot be drawn to worship some idol. In their eyes there is no ground for comparison between the experience of heavenly things and the wicked inventions of men.

15.3.4.en: The inventions of men will not cease, but the children of God are firm in their hope in the Lord, holding fast to the Kingdom of their Father.

15.4.0.en: The sight of it arouses passion in fools, and makes them desire the form of a dead image without spirit. [5]

15.4.1.en: However great the artist's perfection, and however great the allurement, the idol is a dead statue with no spirit in it; how then does a living man enslave himself to a dead statue? It is fitting for man to take pride in what he has received, for there is no ground for comparison between the statue, whatever its allurements, and man, created in the image and likeness of God!

15.5.0.en: Those who make them, and those who desire them, and those who worship them, are lovers of evil, and worthy to have such things as their hopes. [6]

15.5.1.en: The wise man wonders how the lust for evil draws these classes, that is, the makers of statues and the lovers of statues, so that they acquire them and worship them.

15.5.2.en: * The idol worshipper is like a murderer. Do you ask: whom does he kill? There is an aggravated charge against him, for he does not kill a stranger, nor a personal enemy, but kills himself. By what nets is he caught? By his error. By what weapon? By rebellion against God.

15.5.3.en: * Idolatry embraces all crimes, and all crimes embrace idolatry.

15.6.0.en: 7 For the potter, tempering soft earth, fashions every vessel with much labor for our service; yea, of the same clay he makes both the vessels that serve for clean uses, and likewise also all such as serve to the contrary; but what is the use of either sort, the potter himself is the judge. 8 And with misspent labor he molds a vain god of the same clay, he who was himself born of earth a little before, and after a short time returns to the same from which he was taken, when his life that was lent him shall be demanded. 9 Notwithstanding his care is, not that he shall have much labor, nor that his life is short, but he strives to excel goldsmiths and silversmiths, and endeavors to do like the workers in brass, and counts it his glory to make counterfeit things.

15.6.1.en: For the potter toils in kneading the soft clay, and forms everything of what we use.

15.6.2.en: Out of the same clay he makes the vessels designated for clean works and those designated for the opposite, all alike.

15.6.3.en: But the designation of each vessel of both classes goes back to the judgment of the maker of the clay. [7]

15.6.4.en: He spoke before of the carpenter (chs. 13-14), to whom God gave skill and art to make ships for the benefit of mankind, and who turned his skill to making dead idols that shatter and corrupt mankind. Now he speaks of the potter, for whom it is fitting, while kneading the clay, to remember how God created man from clay, so that he may glorify his Creator by his skill and work for the benefit of mankind, and not form a ceramic idol in folly, driving men to unclean practices in their worship of idols!

15.6.5.en: So it is fitting for both the carpenter and the potter to bear witness to the wisdom of God the Savior and Creator, but in folly they turned the thoughts of men from their Creator to worship wooden or ceramic idols.

15.6.6.en: The wise man does not attack carpenters and potters, for all who have skills can work and create for the edification of mankind, bringing out of wood household tools or tools of work, and out of clay clean and splendid vessels used in cooking or serving food and drink or for adornment, and so on.

15.6.7.en: For work in wood and clay and stones and metals is holy if the will of the workers is holy. To the pure all things are pure.

15.6.8.en: * All things that exist are good, because the Creator of all of them is wholly good.

15.6.9.en: St. Augustine * Creatures are not evil by nature; if they were evil God would not have created them, for “every creature of God is good,” as the Apostle Paul said (1 Tim 4:4); and God's commandment does not command us to reject good things and flee from them, but to manage them well. And no one is condemned for possessing wealth, but for boasting in it or for misusing it.

15.6.10.en: St. Basil the Great * Is not the world good? Is not the present life good? But if these draw me away from Christ I count all these things loss. Why? “For the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord.” For when the sun rises, sitting beside a candle is counted a loss. For loss rests on comparison, on the superiority of the other things... Notice how he calls everything loss, not in itself, but for the sake of Christ.

15.7.0.en: St. John Chrysostom And toiling to no purpose he makes of the same clay a trifling god, one born of clay a little while ago, who after a little while returns to the clay from which he was taken, when he is asked to repay the soul that was lent him. [8]

15.7.1.en: The wise man looks at the potter who spends all effort to bring out of clay a god to be worshipped by himself and by him who buys it from him. It is a toilsome effort, and a corruption of thought and of gifts as of life, for the potter to imagine that he is able to bring into being a god made by his hands.

15.7.2.en: Perhaps by his saying “repay the soul that was lent him” he means that Satan enters the statue and speaks and deceives by working miracles as the magicians did before Pharaoh, but only for a while.

15.7.3.en: * By these words (Isa 44:11) God teaches us how great is their folly, for they worship (the idols) as makers of good things... The makers of these which seem gods are men who have the same nature as those who worship them, and the man who makes them himself worships them as a god.

15.8.0.en: Tertullian Yet he does not care that he shall die, and that his life is short, but vies with the goldsmiths and silversmiths, and imitates the workers in brass, and glories in forming counterfeit gods. [9]

15.8.1.en: The makers of idols compete in making statues, and each of them boasts that he has made a god or false gods. In their recklessness they boast of the work of their hands and count them great works, while they trade in religion and seek their own material gain.

15.9.0.en: 10 His heart is ashes, his hope is more vile than earth, and his life of less value than clay, 11 forasmuch as he knew not his Maker, and Him that inspired into him an active soul, and breathed in a living spirit. 12 But they counted our life a pastime, and our time here a market for gain: for, say they, we must be getting every way, though it be by evil means. 13 For this man, more than all others, knows that he offends, in that of earthly matter he makes brittle vessels and graven images.

15.9.1.en: His heart is ashes, and his hope is more vile than earth, and his life more despicable than clay. [10]

15.9.2.en: Since Israel rejected the light of the Lord, He warns them by Isaiah the prophet not to imitate the pagan nations that ignored man's dignity and brought him down to the depths, saying: “Their land also is full of idols; they worship the work of their own hands, that which their own fingers have made: and the mean man bows down, and the great man humbles himself: therefore forgive them not” (Isa 2:8-9).

15.9.3.en: Truly what grieves the heart of God, who created man from the dust and breathed into him the breath of life, and gave him to be in His likeness and image, is that he has sunk to his origin, indeed to what is lower than this origin. By his disobedience to the Spirit of God and his welcoming the thoughts of the devil, making idols to worship, his heart became ashes, lower than dust and of less value. His hope became more despicable than the dust from which he was created, because dust does no evil.

15.9.4.en: * What a terrible thing it is when man leaves the easy yoke of Christ and His light burden (Mt 11:30), and submits to the yoke of demons and bears the weight of exceedingly sinful sin, after we have learned that the heart of idol worshippers is ashes, and their life no more than dust (Wis 15:10).

15.10.0.en: Origen Because he ignored Him who fashioned him, and breathed into him an active soul, and inspired a living spirit. [11]

15.10.1.en: A grave contrast between the work of God who loves man and man who loves evil. God created man and formed him from the dust, but breathed into him the breath of life that gives him the spirit of working with power, to govern the world with holiness and righteousness; and the other supposes that he is able to raise up from dust a god without motion, without life.

15.10.2.en: God wishes to raise man's estate to dwell in heaven and enjoy fellowship in the glories, and man in his degradation wishes to submit to the dust and clay that has no life.

15.10.3.en: * He who was created in the image of God and received authority over all creatures on earth as his portion, fell by his folly from his royal position. And wanting to recover the honors, behold by his own will he honors the work of his hands, and bows down and prostrates himself and submits himself to the despotic authority of the demons.

15.10.4.en: Father Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus * Prostration before God lifts man up and increases his greatness, and bowing before idols lowers his estate and brings him down.

15.10.5.en: What degradation is greater than that man should leave his salvation, and set up enmity with the God of the universe, and at the same time bow before lifeless things, worshipping stones?

15.10.6.en: Truly God raised us by the honor with which He created us to something greater than the heavens, but Satan set it in himself to degrade those who obey him until they become beings without feeling or life. This is surely the reason for which the prophet declares: “The mean man bows down, and the great man humbles himself” (Isa 2:9).

15.10.7.en: St. John Chrysostom But he counted our life a worthless game, and our existence a market of profits, and said:

15.11.0.en: “We must be getting by every means, though it be by evil.” [12]

15.11.1.en: While God wishes to raise man to a surpassing level, so that he may have a portion among the heavenly ones, and it has cost Him much, for He sent the fathers and the prophets and the Law and allowed events to prepare the way for the acceptance of His work of salvation. The matter of man's salvation and glorification is the concern of the Holy Trinity, and still occupies God the Trinity until we enter into glory. Sadly, man sometimes trifles with his salvation, and counts his life a worthless game.

15.11.2.en: While God prepares for us the eternal heavenly glories, behold man is occupied with material gains or temporal honors that he achieves even by unseemly ways such as injustice. For example, Demetrius the silversmith, who made silver shrines for Diana, brought the craftsmen no small gain (Acts 19:24), and caused the Apostle Paul many troubles.

15.11.3.en: The Christian, as he walks on earth in a spirit of responsibility and commitment in all that is entrusted to him, bears a heavenly touch in his thoughts as in his feelings and emotions, translated in his words and outward conduct. Our life is a divine school in which we learn and train for the heavenly life, in all directions of our life.

15.11.4.en: * I want you to keep your minds on these things continually (Col 3:1). For our concern with them frees us from the earth and transports us to heaven.

15.11.5.en: St. John Chrysostom * Though we are surrounded by the world, we do not give ourselves up to it.

15.11.6.en: Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus * The end toward which we strive, and which we aspire to reach with all care and diligence, is the blessed life with God in the immortal heaven. And nothing in the world equals this praiseworthy endeavor in honor and greatness for the rational creation.

15.11.7.en: * Direct your striving toward heaven, and profit from everything you meet on the course of your life on earth.

15.11.8.en: * Asceticism is the loosing of the bonds of this perishing material life, and release from human attachments so that we may prepare ourselves the more to be on the road that leads to God. It is the unhindered impulse to acquire and enjoy the exceedingly precious goods that are “more to be desired than gold, yea, than much fine gold” (Ps 19:10). In short, asceticism is a transfer from the human heart to the heavenly life, so that we may say: “For our conversation is in heaven.” Also it is the chief point, the first step toward being like Christ, who though He was rich, yet for our sakes became poor (2 Cor 8:9). For if we do not obtain this likeness it is impossible for us to reach the way of life according to the Gospel of Christ.

15.11.9.en: * While we drag our body on the earth like a shadow, we keep our souls in the company of the heavenly spirits.

15.12.0.en: St. Basil the Great For he knows better than all men that he offends, because he makes from earthly matter brittle vessels and graven images. [13]

15.12.1.en: However great the folly of the potter, in his depths he realizes as he makes an idol for worship that he is sinning, and that what he makes is breakable and perishable.

15.13.s.en: 5. Exchanging the Immortal for the dead

15.13.0.en: 14 And all the enemies of Your people, who hold them in subjection, are most foolish, and are more miserable than very babies. 15 For they counted all the idols of the heathen to be gods, which neither have the use of eyes to see, nor noses to draw breath, nor ears to hear, nor fingers of hands to handle; and as for their feet, they are slow to go. 16 For man made them, and he that borrowed his own spirit fashioned them: but no man can make a god like unto himself. 17 For being mortal, he works a dead thing with wicked hands: for he himself is better than the things which he worships: whereas he lived once, but they never. 18 Yea, they worshipped those beasts also that are most hateful, for being compared together, some are worse than others. 19 Neither are they beautiful, so much as to be desired in respect of beasts: but they went without the praise of God and His blessing.

15.13.1.en: Some see that he concentrated on Egypt when he referred to the pagan nations, because some of the Egyptians were among the worst idol worshippers.

15.13.2.en: He cast light on the error of the ancient Egyptians in their folly regarding the worship of idols that are lifeless and unable to act.

15.13.3.en: Perhaps the satire here against the idols rests on what is recorded in (Psalm 115:4-7; Psalm 135:15-18).

15.13.4.en: But all the enemies of Your people who rule over it are very foolish, and more wretched than the babies themselves. [14]

15.13.5.en: When man withdraws from God he becomes foolish and ignorant, and enslaves himself to what is mean; he becomes like a child, not in simplicity, but in lack of knowledge and lack of understanding and of studying matters seriously.

15.13.6.en: * Humor (or lack of seriousness) makes the soul pampered and idle, for it stirs up the soul excessively and often causes violent acts and creates wars, and what more than this? In short, do you not wish to be among men? Leave childish things!

15.13.7.en: St. John Chrysostom * Christ does not want us to be without understanding but wants us to understand all that is useful and necessary for our salvation in a perfect manner. For even Wisdom promises that she will give “to the simple subtlety, to the young man knowledge and discretion” (see Prov 1:4). And Wisdom is found in the Book of Proverbs as one who lifts up her voice and says: “Unto you, O men, I call; and my voice is to the sons of man. O you simple, understand wisdom: and you fools, be of an understanding heart” (see Prov 8:4-5)...

15.13.8.en: But how can a man be simple and wise at the same time? This the Savior makes clear to us in another place, saying: “Be therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves” (Mt 10:16); and in the same way the blessed Paul writes: “Brethren, be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be children, but in understanding be men” (1 Cor 14:20).

15.13.9.en: We must examine what it means to be children in malice, and how a man becomes so while being in mind a mature man. A child's knowledge is very little, and sometimes entirely lacking, so he is innocent of the corruption of evil, and it is our duty also to strive to imitate them in this matter by uprooting the habits of evil from us completely, so that we are looked upon as men who have not even knowledge of the way that leads to guile, having no perception of craftiness or deceit, but being simple and innocent, practicing kindness and a humility that is beyond price, and ready to bear anger and malice. By this we affirm that we bear the marks of those who are still children.

15.13.10.en: While our character is simple and innocent, it is fitting for us to be perfect in mind, so that our understanding is established firmly and clearly on Him who is by nature and in truth the Creator of the universe, God the Lord...

15.13.11.en: The chief perfection of the mind rests on faith, so that our understanding is not corrupt; and the second matter, adjoining this chief perfection and near to it and attending it, is the clear knowledge of the way of conduct that pleases God, which we learned by the Gospel, the perfect way that is without blame (here the saint distinguishes between those who walk the evangelical way of the Lord and those who are noble in conduct through philosophies that can deceive). He who walks this way practices a life of simplicity and innocence, and yet they know what (doctrinal) opinions they hold and what true works they practice. Such enter by the narrow gate, and do not reject the labors that are required for godliness in God and necessary to lead to the glorious life. So truly they advance to the wide abundance of the way of God and rejoice in His gifts, and win for themselves the Kingdom of Heaven through Christ, to whom with God the Father be praise and dominion, through Christ, with the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.

15.14.0.en: St. Cyril the Great For they counted all the idols of the Gentiles gods, though they do not use their eyes to see, nor their noses to breathe the air, nor their ears to hear, nor the fingers of their hands to touch, and though their feet are unable to walk. [15]

15.14.1.en: It is strange that the Pharaohs, who excelled in knowledge of the art of embalming and astronomy and architecture and colors and sculpture, and so on, fell into worshipping statues that do not see nor breathe the air nor hear, and have no feeling when someone touches them, unable to move. The Pharaohs, full of vitality and activity, worship what is inert.

15.14.2.en: * How can one not pity them in this respect, when he sees them worshipping what is unable to see, and hears them praying to what is unable to hear, and beholds men like themselves who were born and have life and mind, but call gods those things that have no motion at all, indeed have not life itself? And the strangest of all is that those which they keep under their authority they serve as their masters.

15.14.3.en: St. Athanasius the Apostolic In his book “Against the Pagans” Pope Athanasius the Apostolic says that it would have been better for the idols not to have ears and eyes and noses and fingers, lest the idol worshippers be exposed in that their idols do not hear nor see nor smell nor touch.

15.14.4.en: For he who made them is a man, and he who molded them is a being who was lent a spirit.

15.15.0.en: And it is not within the power of man to make a god like himself. [16]

15.15.1.en: The maker of these idols is the artist man, who with all the skill and art he has reached does not possess life. The breath of life in him is lent to him as a divine gift, and certainly one day he dies and his soul departs from his body; how then does such a being give immortal life to dead materials without life?!

15.16.0.en: And since he is mortal, he makes a dead thing with wicked hands.

15.16.1.en: He himself is one of the things that he worships, for he was alive, but they were not alive. [17]

15.16.2.en: Man is a mortal being, unable to raise himself or return his soul to his body; how then do his hands reach out in iniquity to claim that he sets up a living god, made by his hands, who does not die? And how does he worship an idol of a man like himself, mortal or already dead?

15.16.3.en: * They hate the vile animals and wild beasts and birds and reptiles, and shrink from them, either because of their fierceness or because of their filthiness, yet they carve their images on stone or wood or gold and call them gods. But it would have been better for them to worship the living creatures themselves instead of worshipping their images in stones. But both cases are a vain pretense, for neither the matter nor the image is the cause of the divine indwelling, but it is the skill of the art that summons the divinity... But if the divinity is joined to the statues because of the art, what need is there also of the matter, so long as it is established in men? For if God reveals Himself only because of the art, and if the statues are worshipped as gods for this reason, it would be more correct to worship and serve man, who is the master of the art, because he is also rational and has intelligence.

15.17.0.en: And they worship even the most harmful animals, and the most foolish of animals. [18]

15.18.0.en: And there is not in them what is in the rest of the animals of fair and charming appearance, and they have lacked the praise of God and His blessing. [19]

15.18.1.en: It is a strange thing that man enslaves himself to animals, which are less than man and created for his service, how much more if he chooses from among them the harmful and fierce and ugly ones. As though, while he exalts himself against God the Creator and resists His commandment and even denies His existence, he is ready to submit to harmful and mean creatures!

15.18.2.en: We conclude our discussion of idol worship with what many of the Fathers pointed out, that man is formed according to the possibilities of him whom he worships. He who worships God the Creator enjoys immortality, and he who worships dead idols falls under death and destruction, and as Holy Scripture affirms, those who worship idols become like them: “they have walked after vanity, and are become vain” (Jer 2:5). “They went to Baal-peor, and separated themselves unto that shame; and their abominations were according as they loved” (Hos 9:10).

15.18.3.en: St. Athanasius the Apostolic sees that man in his wickedness sank down the more, so he mixed together dissimilar creatures, the rational with the irrational, like the gods of the Egyptians that have the head of a dog or the head of a serpent or the head of an ass, and Ammon the god of the Libyans who has the head of a ram. And some deified parts of the human body such as the head and the shoulder and the hand and the foot.

15.18.4.en: Why does Holy Scripture sometimes call idols gods?

15.18.5.en: * When Holy Scripture calls them gods, though they are not gods, it does not declare of them that they are gods in any sense, but in an added sense, though it shows that they are not gods at all. As David says: “All the gods of the nations are idols (demons)” (see Ps 96:5).

15.18.6.en: “There shall no strange god be in you” (Ps 81:9). In this he says: gods of the pagans, but the pagans are ignorant of the true God, and it calls the idols “other gods,” in order to repel their view that they are gods. But as to their reality, he says of them “idols (demons),” and Isaiah says: “Let all them be ashamed that blaspheme God and carve things that are profitable for nothing, I am a witness, says God” (see Isa 44:11). And Jeremiah also says the same: “The gods that have not made the heavens and the earth” (Jer 10:11).

15.18.8.en: Your fatherhood keeps me and lifts me up to You!

15.18.9.en: * I look to You, O Wisdom of God; I see You the Sun of Righteousness, shining with the rays of love upon all mankind.

15.18.10.en: * I plunge into the sea of Your mercies and Your longsuffering.

15.18.11.en: So my depths are filled with Your tender fatherhood!

15.18.12.en: * Allow me, O Wisdom of God, to complain to You of myself.

15.18.13.en: For You created me a free lord, and a king, an ambassador of the King of kings.

15.18.14.en: And in my folly I drew my hand away from Your hands.

15.18.15.en: And I turned my eyes away from Your eyes, and my ear was occupied with the voices of the wicked enemy.

15.18.16.en: * I complain to You of my fathers who left You, O Source of wisdom, and descended from the heavenly life to the dunghill.

15.18.17.en: They exchanged You for idols that do not hear nor see nor smell nor move.

15.18.18.en: * How strange! They fear the wild beasts, and set up idols of insects and reptiles.

15.18.19.en: They set up idols for them, and adorn them with roses and precious stones and gold and silver.

15.18.20.en: They exalt themselves in pride and arrogance, and set up statues of emperors and kings, and offer them offerings and sacrifices even after the death of the emperors...

15.18.21.en: * How strange! You took clay and raised me from it, when You breathed into it a breath of life from You.

15.18.22.en: And behold the potter takes clay, and makes a ceramic idol for man to bow down to.

15.18.23.en: You raised us from the dunghill to sit in heaven with the heavenly orders, and by our corrupt will and in our full freedom we came down to bow to the dust!

15.18.24.en: Our fathers exchanged You, O eternal Holy One, for lifeless ceramic!

15.18.25.en: Did our fathers find happiness in humiliation before idols?

15.18.26.en: Does man love degradation and humiliation?

15.18.27.en: * Glory to You, O heavenly Wisdom of God!

15.18.28.en: You came down to us, and lived on our earth, that by Your Cross You might draw us again from the dust to the glories.

15.18.29.en: You emptied Yourself, and took our form, we slaves, that You might lift us from slavery to the glory of the children of God.

15.18.30.en: You opened to us, the earthly ones, the door of heaven, and called the heavenly orders to rejoice in us.

15.18.31.en: * You made us a wonder before the heavenly ones!

15.18.32.en: Behold all heaven awaits the day of Your coming on the clouds, to see all Your believers, the heavenly Queen, enjoying a marvelous and surpassing glory!
